name: Prize crossword No 24,141
preamble: Solve the clues and fit the solutions into the grid, jigsaw-wise, wherever they will go. This week's Prize puzzle has special instructions; the clues are not assigned numbers so you need to fit the answers into the grid yourself. Disregard the numbers in the grid.

clue.text: Cowboy work playing lyre with bird in jug

indicators.note: playing with something means toying with it, so the letters are moved around freely

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cowboy strums a lyre while a bird sits in a jug, a cheerful campfire scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cowboy' is not the Wild West here: in Britain a cowboy is a shoddy, unqualified tradesman. 'Lyre with bird' also hides the lyrebird, an Australian songbird, inside the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Jerry-building means putting up houses cheaply and badly, exactly the slapdash construction a rogue tradesman delivers.

clue.text: Duck towards the floor to keep warm

definitions.note: the clue gives a purpose; the answer is the quilt that serves it

blocks.note: the eider is a large sea duck
downwards, towards the floor

explanation.surface: Someone ducks low to the ground to stay warm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duck' looks like a verb meaning to crouch, but it is the bird. The definition is loose: it names what the answer is for rather than the thing itself.
explanation.definitionFit: An eiderdown is a thick quilt stuffed with soft feathers, laid over a bed to hold in heat at night.

clue.text: Sound of light in lift

indicators.note: the sound of something is what reaches the ear, so we want a word said the same way

blocks.note: rays are beams of light

explanation.surface: The hum of the light bulb inside an elevator car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lift' reads as the British word for an elevator, but it is the verb. Beams of light are rays, which is said exactly like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To raise something is to move it upward, a plain synonym for hoisting or elevating it.

clue.text: Standard American? Not the real thing

blocks.note: from the British phrase bog-standard, meaning ordinary or basic
US is the standard abbreviation for American

explanation.surface: An ordinary American is dismissed as a fake.
explanation.walkthrough: Bog-standard is everyday British slang for plain and unremarkable, so the first word of the phrase stands in for 'standard'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something bogus is counterfeit or sham, a fake pretending to be genuine.

clue.text: Lustrously adorned listener was first to follow fiend

blocks.note: an imp is a small devil
the ear is the organ that listens
to lead is to be in front

explanation.surface: A gleaming eavesdropper got in first, ahead of some demon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To follow fiend' puts the listener and the leading after the devil, so the imp comes first even though it is named last.
explanation.definitionFit: Impearled is a poetic word for decked with pearls or pearl-like drops, so shining with gems.

clue.text: Pickpocket gets hard strap at start of E, for example

blocks.note: dip is old slang for a pickpocket
H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard
a thong is a leather strap

explanation.surface: A thief collects a stiff strap at the start of some route marked E.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a teasing example: many words starting with E open on two blended vowels, as in eye, Euro or eight.
explanation.definitionFit: A diphthong is a vowel sound gliding between two positions, the kind of blended sound heard opening words like eye.

clue.text: Bottom of screen a director uses

indicators.note: what a phrase uses is part of what it contains, so the letters sit inside the words

blocks.note: the run of letters spanning the end of the first word, the whole second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: The lower edge of the cinema screen that a film director works with.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer straddles three words, from the last letter of 'screen' into the start of 'director'.
explanation.definitionFit: The nadir is the lowest point of anything, a figurative synonym for rock bottom.

clue.text: Fitter but ...

definitions.note: an adjective; the answer is what makes one fitter for a post

blocks.note: first meaning: a certificate or skill that makes someone more fit for a job
second meaning: a reservation or proviso, which is what a 'but' introduces

explanation.walkthrough: The trailing dots make the clue look unfinished; each of the two words is a meaning of the answer, with a 'but' being a hedge added to a statement.
explanation.definitionFit: The word covers both an attainment that makes a person suitable and a limiting condition attached to a claim.

clue.text: Indicator on plan for decimal currency when St Hugh first topped tyrant

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept
to top something is to cut off its head, so the opening letter is removed

blocks.note: X is the Roman numeral for ten
the mark was the German currency
taken as written
opening letter of the name
a despot is a tyrant; here it loses its head

explanation.surface: A treasure map marks where decimal coinage arrived after a saint overthrew a despot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Decimal currency' looks like one idea but splits into a ten and a mark. The answer is then re-divided across new word breaks.
explanation.definitionFit: On a treasure map the cross shows where to dig, so the stock phrase names the marker on a plan.

clue.text: Immortal student leaving island in Gabon

indicators.note: whoever is leaving departs, so that letter goes out of the word

blocks.note: Lundy, an island in the Bristol Channel off south-west England
L, the learner plate letter, is the deleted piece
taken as written
G is Gabon's international vehicle registration code

explanation.surface: An eternal scholar leaves an island to settle in an African country.
explanation.walkthrough: Lundy is a small island off Devon. 'In Gabon' looks like a location but is two pieces: the word itself and the country's car-sticker code.
explanation.definitionFit: Undying means never dying or fading, the same everlasting quality as being immortal.

clue.text: Pontificate over fashion for the people

indicators.note: turned over means flipped round, so the word is read backwards

blocks.note: pop is short for popular, of the people
a mode is a fashion

explanation.surface: Someone holds forth at length about fashion for the masses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pontificate' reads as the verb meaning to sound off, but here it is the noun: a pope's office or reign.
explanation.definitionFit: A pontificate is the office and term of a pope, which is exactly what popedom denotes.

clue.text: Elgar's work is great

indicators.note: a composer's work is something produced, so the letters are worked into a new form

blocks.note: the English composer's name

explanation.surface: A music lover declares that a piece by Elgar is magnificent.
explanation.walkthrough: Edward Elgar was an English composer; his surname rearranges neatly into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Large and great both describe something big in size or extent, a straightforward synonym pair.

clue.text: I disperse people from t-terraces

indicators.note: something made from raw material is formed out of it, so the letters are remade

blocks.note: the stammered word keeps its extra T

explanation.surface: A steward stammers that they clear the crowd off the football terraces.
explanation.walkthrough: The stutter in 't-terraces' is not decoration: the extra T is needed for the letter count. The definition is in the first person, so the answer describes the speaker.
explanation.definitionFit: One who disperses a crowd sends it in all directions, which makes that person a scatterer of people.

clue.text: Plants liquid gold on part of Alaska

indicators.note: only a part is taken, here the opening letter alone

blocks.note: fl. is the abbreviation for fluid
or is gold in heraldry
opening letter of the state

explanation.surface: Vegetation drips with molten gold somewhere in Alaska, evoking the gold rush.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Liquid gold' looks like one phrase, perhaps oil, but splits into the fluid abbreviation and the heraldic word.
explanation.definitionFit: Flora is the collective term for the plant life of a region, as fauna is for animals.

clue.text: Wit takes room for season

blocks.note: an attic is a room under the roof
salt is what we use for seasoning food

explanation.surface: A comedian books a room for the summer season.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Season' reads as a time of year, but it is the verb, to flavour food.
explanation.definitionFit: Attic salt is a literary phrase for refined, elegant humour, after the dry wit of ancient Athens.

clue.text: Game's outside base at festival

indicators.note: to be outside something is to surround it, so one piece wraps another

blocks.note: halma is a board game, and the 's is kept
base means low or mean

explanation.surface: A game played outdoors at a base camp during a holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: Halma is a Victorian board game played by jumping pieces; the possessive gives the final S.
explanation.definitionFit: Hallowmas is the old name for All Saints' Day on 1 November, a church feast day.

clue.text: Combine runner without zephyr with leader of run

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so one piece goes around another
the leader is the one at the front, so the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: a hare is a fast runner
a zephyr is a very light vest or undershirt
opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone tries to merge a sprinter, a breeze and a team leader into one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like 'lacking', but it means outside. A zephyr is a gentle breeze, and also a thin vest. 'Combine' is the farm machine, not the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A combine is short for combine harvester, the farm machine that reaps and threshes grain.

clue.text: Preserve and spoil invalid over water

blocks.note: to mar is to spoil
French for sick, as a seasick traveller is, from mal de mer

explanation.surface: Someone ruins things by preserving a sick person who is at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Invalid' is the noun, a sick person; the setter borrows the French word for one, who is sick over the water in mal de mer.
explanation.definitionFit: Marmalade is a citrus jam, and a preserve is any fruit cooked with sugar to keep.

clue.text: Senior officer's half turn towards danger when surrounded

indicators.note: only half the word survives, so its second part is cut away

blocks.note: C-in-C, Commander-in-Chief
the first half of the word, its opening two letters, with the rest deleted
red is the colour of danger

explanation.surface: A general makes a half turn towards danger after being surrounded by the enemy.
explanation.walkthrough: C-in-C, Commander-in-Chief, is the standard shorthand for the top officer.
explanation.definitionFit: A cincture is a girdle or belt, so cinctured means encircled or girdled round.

clue.text: Width on horse?

blocks.note: first meaning: the measurement around the middle of something
second meaning: the band under a horse's belly that holds the saddle

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark asks whether 'on horse' is fair as a definition: it describes where the strap sits rather than naming it.
explanation.definitionFit: Girth means both a body's circumference and the saddle strap buckled round a horse's middle.

clue.text: Local officer, zany Saracen to Spooner if American

indicators.note: Dr Spooner famously swapped the starts of words, so the opening sounds trade places

blocks.note: a zany is a clown; after the swap of opening sounds it comes out as this word
a Saracen is loosely a Turk; swapped, and said the American way, it comes out as this word

explanation.surface: A council official is described as a wild crusader enemy, at least by Spooner in the US.
explanation.walkthrough: 'If American' matters: in British speech the second word sounds like 'clark', but Americans say 'clurk', which rhymes with the Saracen.
explanation.definitionFit: A town clerk is the official who keeps records and handles business for a town council.

clue.text: A question of place

blocks.note: surface reading: a matter of position or social rank
setter's reading: the question word one asks about location

explanation.walkthrough: 'A question of place' sounds like an issue of status or etiquette; read literally, it is the interrogative that asks for a location.
explanation.definitionFit: The interrogative is used to ask about location, so it is literally the question asked about a place.

clue.text: Job's second piece of work has a lot of green cloth backing

indicators.note: a piece is one small bit, here the closing letter alone
a lot but not all, so one letter is dropped
going backwards, so the letters run in the opposite direction

blocks.note: closing letter of the word
baize, the green cloth on snooker tables, losing its first letter

explanation.surface: A biblical sufferer's second job involves plenty of green cloth fabric.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Job' looks like work, which the clue reinforces, but it is the biblical Job, whose second daughter after his trials was Keziah (Job 42:14).
explanation.definitionFit: The Book of Job names his three later daughters Jemima, Kezia and Keren-happuch, so she is the second.

clue.text: Bottles for little girl without love as well

indicators.note: without means lacking, so that letter is taken away

blocks.note: Vi is a short form of Violet
also, minus the O
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O; this is the letter removed

explanation.surface: Feeding bottles for a small girl who also lacks affection.
explanation.walkthrough: Love means nil in tennis scoring, which crosswords read as the letter O.
explanation.definitionFit: Vials are small glass containers for liquids such as medicine, so they are little bottles.

clue.text: Love of our neighbour

blocks.note: first meaning: the Roman goddess of love
second meaning: the planet next to Earth

explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like the commandment to love one's neighbour; instead 'our' means Earth's.
explanation.definitionFit: The name belongs both to the Roman goddess of love and to the planet whose orbit lies next to Earth's.

clue.text: Month in which girl wants ham

indicators.note: something in which another sits holds it, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: OCT is the calendar abbreviation for October
a girl's name

explanation.surface: There is a month when a girl craves ham, perhaps Christmas ham.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ham' looks like food but is the verb: to perform with exaggerated gestures.
explanation.definitionFit: To ham is to perform in an exaggerated, theatrical way, which is to overplay a role.

clue.text: Traveller does a bit of whizzing around

indicators.note: only a bit of the phrase is used, a stretch of consecutive letters inside it

blocks.note: the run starting in the middle of the first word and ending early in the second

explanation.surface: A traveller zips about a little.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Around' looks like it should turn the letters back, but it is just part of the fodder; the answer reads forwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Zingaro is the Italian word for a Romani person, a member of a traditionally nomadic people.

clue.text: Has-beens in country seats with dry rot

indicators.note: rotting things fall apart and decompose, so the letters break up and re-form
one piece placed in another sits inside it

blocks.note: the country on the Arabian peninsula
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Faded aristocrats sit in decaying country houses riddled with dry rot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Country seats' wants to be stately homes; it splits into a nation and plain seats. 'Dry rot' likewise splits into fodder and the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Yesterday's men are people whose time of influence is over, the idiomatic equivalent of washed-up has-beens.
